summary:
Our Project, MARSCOPE is an interactive Mars exploration platform integrating planetary datasets, geospatial analysis, atmospheric visualization, and experimental A*-based pathfinding for Jezero Crater 
exploration.

Objective
To analyse Jezero Crater's terrain and environmental conditions, supporting research and terrain-aware planetary exploration.

Methods & Data
Uses USGS CTX imagery and DEMs for surface and slope analysis, THEMIS day/night infrared mosaics for thermal context, and Montabone et al.'s MY36 Dust Scenario V2.5, based on Mars Climate Sounder observations, for dust visualization. Perseverance landmarks provide mission context.

What We Developed
A web prototype with six modules: surface exploration, atmospheric visualization, mission landmarks, terrain intelligence, A\* route planning, and simulated science targets. Features include interactive maps, terrain statistics, slope classifications, infrared and dust layers, and shortest-distance versus slope-weighted route comparisons.

How Does It Address the Challenge
Combines fragmented planetary datasets into one accessible platform for exploring surface conditions, analysing terrain, visualizing environmental context, and testing routes.

Why Is It Important
Demonstrates how geospatial integration, scientific visualization, and computational methods can advance planetary research, support future exploration planning, and make Mars science more accessible.
details:
MARSCOPE

MARSCOPE is an interactive planetary exploration platform focused on Jezero Crater, Mars. It integrates scientific planetary datasets into a unified interface for exploring surface features, terrain conditions, atmospheric dust, thermal context, and experimental exploration routes.

How it works
The platform combines USGS CTX imagery and Digital Elevation Models (DEM) for surface and slope analysis, THEMIS day/night infrared mosaics for thermal visualization, and Montabone et al.'s MY36 Dust Scenario V2.5 for atmospheric dust context. It also incorporates documented Perseverance mission landmarks. DEM-derived slope analysis identifies terrain patterns, while an experimental A* algorithm compares shortest-distance and slope-weighted routes.

Benefits & Intended Impact
MARSCOPE reduces the fragmentation of planetary datasets by bringing multiple scientific sources into one accessible environment. It helps users understand Martian terrain and environmental conditions, explore mission locations, and experiment with terrain-aware route planning. Its intended impact is to support planetary research, improve accessibility to scientific data, and demonstrate computational approaches for future exploration missions.

Tools & Technologies
Developed as a Python-based Streamlit web application using geospatial processing, raster analysis, mapping, data visualization, and pathfinding libraries. It uses publicly available USGS, NASA/JPL, THEMIS, and Mars Climate Sounder-related datasets. No specialized hardware was required beyond a development computer.

Creativity & Innovation
The project's creativity lies in combining surface, thermal, atmospheric, and terrain intelligence into one interactive planetary exploration system. Its integration of scientific visualization with comparative A* pathfinding transforms static planetary datasets into an exploratory decision-support prototype.

Factors Considered:
We considered scientific data reliability, spatial resolution, coordinate consistency, missing elevation values, computational efficiency, usability, and the limitations of derived classifications. Routes and terrain categories are experimental and are not certified for operational rover navigation.
